sections.section_title: 1. Epidemiology and Pathophysiology of Abdominal Masses in Pregnancy
sections.description: This section sets the clinical context for why abdominal masses can arise during gestation and what mechanisms drive their development.
subtopics: Prevalence of uterine leiomyomas during pregnancy
Physiologic enlargement versus pathologic mass formation
Possible etiologies: decidualised endometrioma versus cystic leiomyoma
Risk factors linked to maternal age, obesity, and parity
Mechanical effects on uterus and surrounding organs

sections.description: The focus here is on how the patient’s history and bedside examination led clinicians toward suspecting an abdominal mass problem.
subtopics: Gestational age assessment and baseline prenatal screening
"Acute" pain distribution – left upper quadrant versus pelvis
"Dyspnoea" stemming from mechanical compression rather than pulmonary pathology
"Vitals" – normal oxygen saturation, heart rate, blood pressure despite abdominal distension
"Bimanual vaginal exam" revealing a fixed hard pelvic lesion extending into the posterior fornix
"Response" to analgesics and positional changes indicating diaphragmatic impingement

sections.description: "This portion describes how imaging modalities complemented laboratory data to distinguish benign from potentially malignant lesions when routine tests were limited in pregnancy."
subtopics: "Ultrasound" features – two large unilocular cysts with peripheral vascularisation;
"Non‑contrast MRI" characteristics – thick walls (1·4 cm), fatty‐sat T1/T2 heterogeneity with focal hyperintense solid spots;
"Tumour markers" – trend analysis of CA‑125 compared with gestational age averages;
"Limitations" inherent to performing these tests during gestation (“first trimester rise”, “non‑specificity”);
"Integration" of US + MRI data highlighting continuity between caudal lesion and posterior myometrium
